Conclusions: The low inflation environment and the outlook for inflation Our analysis concludes that, despite the commonality of experience across countries, the effects of globalisation on inflation has been overall contained. The most intuitive explanation is that the concurrent inflation decline across advanced economies is due to (1) the monetary policy strategies adopted by the central banks of advanced economies over those years; (2) the wage concertation mechanisms consistent with those strategies (i.e. lower wage indexation); and (3) the consequent stabilisation of expectations. Overall, while globalisation has had profound effects on the world economy and affected the inflation process in advanced economies to some extent, it has not significantly impeded the ECBs ability to achieve price stability autonomously. Title: How prepared is the Slovenian banking system to deal with current risks and future challenges?
Subtitle: Delo, Sobotna priloga, 16. oktober 2021  dr. Primo Dolenc, namestnik guvernerja, Banka Slovenije, dr. Meta Ahtik, direktorica oddelka Finanna stabilnost in makrobonitetna politika, Banka Slovenije
text: How ready is the Slovenian banking system to deal with current risks and future challenges? 10/18/2021 / Public apperances Work, Saturday Annex, 16 October 2021  Dr. Primoz Dolenc, Deputy Governor, Banka Slovenije, Dr. Meta Ahtik, Director of The Financial Stability and Macro-Prudential Policy Department, Bank of Slovenia The recovery of the Slovenian, European and global economies in recent quarters continues to be accompanied by uncertainty about the continuation of the epidemic. In this context, the stance of the euro area monetary policy remains accommodative, while withdrawing some of the other measures that we have taken in support of the population and businesses in the context of the initial waves of the epidemic. As the economy recovers, the conditions of the banks have also improved. Macroeconomic and credit risk has been gradually weakening in recent quarters as the economy recovers, but with uncertainty about the continuation of the epidemic, the macroeconomic and credit risks remain heightened. The overall level of risk is decreasing slightly in the past few quartile estimates, while at the same time they are more exposed to other risks than in the recent past. In the face of high growth in house prices, the risk arising from the property market has been strengthened. However, the banking system also faces increased income risk and the challenge of long-term sustainability of profitability, in the face of current challenges. This will be the most marked by the business of both Slovenian and European banks in the medium term. In October, banka Slovenije carried out a re-regular assessment of the situation in our [1] banking system and published our findings in the new Financial Stability Report. The content is explained in more detail below. Note: When showing risks and resilience, the color scale rating refers to an estimate up to one quarter in advance. The arrow represents an expected change in risk or resistance on a scale (up or down) over a slightly longer horizon, around one year. For the risks of pointing the up arrow (downwards) means increasing (reducing) the risk and strengthening it in the case of resistance. The demonstration of risks and resilience in the banking sector is based on an analysis of key risks and resilience for the Slovenian banking system and is defined as a set of quantitative and qualitative indicators for the definition and measurement of systemic risk and resilience. The April Financial Stability Report changed the treatment of income risk by highlighting in particular the risk of generating (net) banks' income, while profitability is shown in the Banking System's resilience to systemic risks along with solvency. Impairments and provisions, or their contribution to the consumption of banks' generated (gross) income, are now only addressed in the credit risk chapter. The reason for the change is the methodological elimination of the double treatment of risks in income and credit risk. The profitability of the banking system is commented on in the extended Solvency and Profitability chapter, assessing the impact of trends in profitability on the resilience of the banking system. A description of the individual risks and resilience is given in the Annex. Source: Banka Slovenije Macroeconomic conditions are improving The situation in the world and here has generally improved in recent months. The global economy is recovering rapidly and has already exceeded the level of gross domestic product from before the start of the pandemic. Based on current data, we estimate that pre-crisis levels could also be reached in Slovenia in the third quarter of 2021. However, the rate of recovery in the event of new outbreaks of infections, the emergence of new strains of the virus and different levels of vaccination remains uncertain and varies from country to country. The even faster moderation of macroeconomic risk on the supply side is being dampened by disruptions in international trade due to bottlenecks in supply chains and a lack of certain production inputs. The risks to the recovery are also posed by the strong rise in commodity prices and the rising consumer price growth, which is otherwise expected to be of a transity nature. Economic activity improved in europe and Slovenia in the second quarter. The start of mass vaccination in the first half of this year has allowed a significant relaxation of restrictive measures. As a whole, GDP growth in the second quarter in the euro area was almost 14%, while in Slovenia it was still two percentage points higher. In our wider surroundings and in our area, economic growth is broadly based, but most of all private consumption has been very low since the start of the pandemic, with the exception of last summer months. However, this factor is not the only factor: as confidence indicators improve, they are reviving investment, and export demand is also important. The economy, supported by economic policy support measures, has maintained its productive potential while improving the outlook for future growth. The risks remain, however, as Slovenia entered a new wave of pandemics in the autumn. This is also more intense due to comparatively lower vaccination rates than in most other euro area members. However, a vaccine is now available, which is increasing the proportion of vaccinated, however slow but increasing. There is also currently no indistri in place to exacerbate the health situation so much that it should be re-encroaching on strict restrictive measures affecting certain parts of the economy, in particular the service sector. At the same time, many industries were able to adapt their business and would not be affected by any restrictive measures as they did in previous epidemiological waves. These factors improve the outlook for this and next year. Our latest assessment for the euro area, which we have made for the euro area, shows that economic growth will reach 5% and would exceed 4% even in a tightened scenario. With the overall recovery of the global economy, especially our trading partners, the reduction of uncertainty and the acceleration of private consumption, the relaxation of restrictive measures, the outlook for Slovenia is even better, as our June forecast already indicated that this year's economic growth will exceed 5%. However, the latest favourable data, as well as some recent forecasts, suggest that growth could also be higher this year. In the medium term, economic growth may be slowed by the aforementioned supply chain disruptions. Successful policy response to the crisis so far The measures that economic policy makers have taken over the last 18 months have proved successful. Monetary policy has been going on for a long time and will remain accommodative for some time to ensure abundant liquidity and favourable financing conditions for both the banking and non-banking sectors and the countries of the Eurosystem. At the same time, with encouraging results, some other measures are gradually being withdrawn, in particular measures of a fiscal nature or measures that we have taken at a time of tightening the situation as a result of the pandemic to support the economy and to ensure financial stability. Thus, even in the first half of this year, we considered that a systemic measure of more favourable regulatory treatment of credit default deferrals was no longer necessary. However, on the basis of in-depth analyses and in line with the decisions we have also taken at European level, at the end of August, we decided not to extend the macro-prudential measure that limited banks and savings banks in tighter economic conditions until the end of September, and recommended that companies moderate the distribution of profits, thereby strengthening the resilience of the financial system to the realisation of risks, in particular credit. Highlighted other risks than in the recent past In light of the current situation in the wider macroeconomic environment and the situation and trends in the financial system, we carried out a regular assessment of the risks in the financial system. For the entire European environment, as well as specifically for the Slovenian financial system, we estimate that the overall level of risks is somewhat decreasing compared to our estimates over the past few quartious studies, while also finding that we need to focus our attention on other risks than in the recent past. As macroeconomic conditions improve and the economic recovery re-emerge, macroeconomic and credit risk is decreasing in the European environment, while risks arising from developments in the financial markets and the real estate market have increased in recent months. The risks arising from the real estate market are increased The latter also applies to Slovenia, where the population in particular sees few serious alternatives to the storage of saved funds in the form of deposits with banks, with the exception of the purchase of real estate. Annual house price growth in the first quarter of this year thus exceeded the European average by almost two percentage points, with only eight European Union countries having higher growth rates. In the second quarter, however, house price growth accelerated further, reaching almost 10%. Slovenia is still the case that price growth in the real estate market, with otherwise increased demand, also indicated by favourable confidence indicators and encouraged by low interest rates, the introduction of slots and banks and an expansional fiscal policy, is importantly determined in particular by limited supply. Slovenia remains close to the bottom of the countries of the European Union in terms of number of dwellings per thousand inhabitants, while the share of new constructions in the total real estate stock is among the lowest (in both cases only four countries lag behind us, with all that stand out according to the first indicator, ahead of Slovenia after the second, which means that they are improving faster than Slovenia). In 2020, investment in residential real estate as a percentage of gross domestic product was as much as three percentage points below the European Union average, with a backlog over a longer period. While annual growth in construction in the european union countries was positive in the first quarter (according to the most recent data of an indicative 2%), in Slovenia it was negative (almost -5%), with only seven countries of the European Union having this parameter worse than Slovenia. In the medium term, the supply may be somewhat strengthened by new construction, as a relatively high number of building permits for residential buildings were issued in the first half of 2021, including a higher proportion of multi-dwelling buildings than in previous periods. Given the exceptionally high proportion of empty properties, the highest among the Members of the European Union (part of these properties are likely to be rented) for which data are available, incentives would be very useful to bring these properties either to the (legal) rental or to the sales market. Income risk remains elevated Notwithstanding the decline in the overall level of risks in the financial system and the slight shift in the hierarchy or importance of individual risks in Slovenia, certain challenges of the past remain present. As a result, some of the risks of our banking system are also unchanged or even have an increase in the near future. In this context, the most pronounced income risk or the challenge of sufficient income generation of banks relates to the individual elements of income generation and cost management. It also links to the resilience of the banking system, and not least to credit risk. In search of higher returns, banks can start to take on (too)high risks. For the banking system, the ability to generate adequate profits is crucial, which maintains the capital capacity of banks in both normal economic conditions and moderate credit growth and stress situations. The net interest margin of Slovenian banks was at the level of the european Union countries in 2020, but has fallen by almost one percentage point in the last 15 years from 2.44% to 1.45%. The increase in credit volumes in the years before the outbreak did not significantly strengthen interest income, and non-interest income could not compensate for the loss of interest, which is also reflected in the profitability of the banking system. This is excellent for us at first sight for the European situation, as our banks reached number one in the European Union last year with over 10% average profitability. However, a detailed insight into the factors of this profitability shows a rather undercuneed picture: a significant part of the profit made falls on one-off factors. Last year, more than 40% of profits came from the "accounting impact" of the merger of the two banks, and this year the decommissioning of past impairments and provisions contributed to the profit made. In the six months this year, our banks made more than 250 million in profits, but half of the increase in profits compared to last year, when it amounted to just over 130 million, stems from the decommissioning of impairments and provisions. In other words: this year the return on capital of Slovenian banks would fall to only a third of the achieved, even if impairments and provisions were at the level of the long-term average, without exceptional years of their formation or decommissioning. The policy of easing impairments was rare among European banks in the first, less optimistic quarter of this year. In addition to the Slovenian banking system, which also last year formed relatively little weakening, only three others were released in the European Union. Credit risk decreased but not negligible The release of impairments and provisions points to a reduced perception of credit risk at banks. In Banka Slovenije, credit risk is also assessed as slightly reduced compared to previous periods, but still increased, as the indicators we monitor have several conflicting trends. Banks' non-profitable exposures are further reduced at already low levels, and banks are reclassing exposures into lower credit risk groups. On the other hand, certain indicators point to a still-present increased credit risk. The shares of non-performing loans are significantly higher in loans with undue deferrals than in the rest of the portfolio. Furthermore, the proportions of under-affordable loans and loans in a group with increased credit risk are increasing in individual activities of non-financial corporations and in certain types of clients or loans. Activities that have been more affected by epidemic-limiting measures stand out, in particular catering and recreation, culture and entertainment. The same applies to independent professions ("craftsmen") and consumer loans. Long-term challenges related to banks' business models In the short term, despite the improvement in the situation, banks' profitability can also be chromium risk, while stable net income generation is crucial for the long-term viability of banks. This brings us to the dilemma facing the entire European banking environment: is the banking business still of interest to investors providing an important component to the banking system  capital? Will competitive pressures, adjustments to the operations of banks and owners' strategies lead to structural changes that will ensure the stability of individual banks and the whole financial system in the long term? In Slovenia, we have a relatively small local market in the process of more or less a universal business model of banking, but even within this model, differences can be formed that serve all stakeholders well, especially banking users and owners. The consolidation of our banking system, which has been going on for several years, will undoubtedly contribute to the reduction in the cost of doing business for the banks, but may already lead to an optimum or limit when further concentration will no longer bring benefits for financial stability, efficiency and users of banking services. Opportunities in digital business and the Green Agenda Pandemic showed where banks still have opportunities, especially in terms of digital business and different sales channels. Like other economic operators, banks have been forced to digitise more, but still have not shown significant progress in the use of modern technologies compared to 2019, as the banks themselves surveyed. Cooperation with fintech companies is likely to bring more advantages compared to competition, while banks must take advantage of their key advantage over entities operating primarily or exclusively digitally  personal knowledge of their long-standing customers, which brings soft information that remotely service entities do not have. Last but not least, there is a green agenda that, once again, after the pandemic situation has eased: European, including our banks, can take an important step in terms of our green transformation in the specific structure of the financial system, where their financial intermediation prevails. Since the strategic reflection, banks have already taken the first steps towards developing green products, but in the coming years they will need to consider even more closely which projects they will fund to maintain the trust and reputation of their owners and customers as well as the regulator. Supervisors and holders of regulatory or rules of conduct of banks are naturally adjusting to current trends or in our operations we are trying to anticipate future challenges. Accordingly, our attention is being paid to micro-prudential supervision and the prudential rules that we set for the operations of banks. But our macroprudentic policy is also adapting. Thus, as of October, banka Slovenije's set of macroprudent measures has been reduced to four active instruments, the assessment of which is still regularly carried out. Careful reflection on the set of measures and the focus of our action is always based on the mandate that has been entrusted to us. [1] Banka Slovenije, Financial Stability Report, October 2021,
text_original: Kako pripravljen je slovenski banni sistem za spopad s trenutnimi tveganji in prihodnjimi izzivi? 10/18/2021 / Public apperances Delo, Sobotna priloga, 16. oktober 2021  dr. Primo Dolenc, namestnik guvernerja, Banka Slovenije, dr. Meta Ahtik, direktorica oddelka Finanna stabilnost in makrobonitetna politika, Banka Slovenije Okrevanje slovenskega, evropskega in svetovnega gospodarstva v zadnjih etrtletjih e naprej spremlja negotovost glede nadaljnjega poteka epidemije. V teh razmerah naravnanost denarne politike evrskega obmoja ostaja spodbujevalna, medtem ko umikamo nekatere druge ukrepe, ki smo jih ob zaetnih valovih epidemije sprejeli v podporo prebivalstvu in podjetjem. Z okrevanjem gospodarstva so se izboljali tudi pogoji poslovanja bank. Makroekonomsko in kreditno tveganje v zadnjih etrtletjih z okrevanjem gospodarstva postopoma slabita, a ob e vedno prisotni negotovosti glede nadaljnjega poteka epidemije ostajata poveani. Sploni nivo tveganj se glede na nae ocene v preteklih nekaj kvartalih nekoliko zmanjuje, hkrati pa so bolj izpostavljena druga tveganja kot v blinji preteklosti. Ob visoki rasti cen stanovanjskih nepreminin se je okrepilo predvsem tveganje, ki izhaja z nepremininskega trga. Banni sistem pa se ob aktualnih izzivih sooa tudi s poveanim dohodkovnim tveganjem in izzivom dolgorone vzdrnosti dobikonosnosti. To bo srednjerono najbolj zaznamovalo poslovanje tako slovenskih kot tudi evropskih bank. V Banki Slovenije smo v oktobru opravili ponovno redno presojo razmer v naem [1] bannem sistemu in nae ugotovitve objavili v novem Poroilu o nanni stabilnosti. Vsebino podrobneje pojasnjujemo v nadaljevanju. Opomba: Pri prikazu tveganj in odpornosti se ocena na barvni lestvici nanaa na oceno do enega etrtletja vnaprej. Puica predstavlja priakovano spremembo tveganja oziroma odpornosti na lestvici (navzgor ali navzdol) v nekoliko daljem horizontu, okrog enega leta. Pri tveganjih usmeritev puice navzgor (navzdol) pomeni poveanje (zmanjanje) tveganja, pri odpornosti pa njeno krepitev (slabitev). Prikaz tveganj in odpornosti v bannem sektorju temelji na analizi kljunih tveganj in odpornosti za slovenski banni sistem ter je opredeljen kot sklop kvantitativnih in kvalitativnih kazalnikov za opredelitev in merjenje sistemskega tveganja in odpornosti. V aprilskem Poroilu o nanni stabilnosti se je spremenila obravnava dohodkovnega tveganja tako, da izpostavlja predvsem tveganje ustvarjanja (neto) dohodka bank, medtem ko je dobikonosnost prikazana v delu Odpornost bannega sistema na sistemska tveganja skupaj s solventnostjo. Oslabitve in rezervacije oziroma njihov prispevek k porabi ustvarjenega (bruto) dohodka bank se zdaj obravnavajo le v poglavju o kreditnem tveganju. Razlog spremembe je metodoloki -odprava podvojene obravnave tveganj v dohodkovnem in kreditnem tveganju. Dobikonosnost bannega sistema komentiramo v razirjenem poglavju Solventnost in dobikonosnost, pri emer ocenimo vpliv gibanj v dobikonosnosti na odpornost bannega sistema. Opis posameznih tveganj in odpornosti je v prilogi. Vir: Banka Slovenije Makroekonomske razmere se izboljujejo Razmere v svetu in pri nas so se v zadnjih mesecih v splonem izboljale. Svetovno gospodarstvo hitro okreva in je e preseglo raven bruto domaega proizvoda iz obdobja pred zaetkom pandemije. Na podlagi tekoih podatkov ocenjujemo, da bi predkrizno raven lahko v tretjem etrtletju 2021 dosegli tudi v Sloveniji. Hitrost okrevanja pa ob novih izbruhih okub, pojavu novih sevov virusa in razlinih ravneh precepljenosti ostaja negotova in se med dravami razlikuje. e hitreje umirjanje makroekonomskega tveganja na ponudbeni strani sicer zavirajo motnje v mednarodni trgovini zaradi ozkih grl v dobavnih verigah in pomanjkanja nekaterih inputov proizvodnje. Tveganje okrevanju predstavljata tudi velika rast cen surovin in vse vija rast cen ivljenjskih potrebin, za katero se sicer priakuje, da bo le prehodne narave. Gospodarska aktivnost se je v drugem etrtletju izboljala tako v Evropi kot tudi Sloveniji. Zaetek mnoinega cepljenja v prvi polovici letonjega leta je namre omogoil precejnjo sprostitev omejitvenih ukrepov. Tako je bila rast BDP v drugem etrtletju v evrskem obmoju skoraj 14 %, v Sloveniji pa e dve odstotni toki vija. V nai iri okolici in tudi pri nas je gospodarska rast iroko osnovana, najve pa k pospeitvi rasti prispeva zasebna potronja, ki je bila v asu od zaetka pandemije, z izjemo lanskih poletnih mesecev, zelo okrnjena. Vendar ta dejavnik ni edini: ob izboljanju kazalnikov zaupanja oivljajo investicije, pomembno je tudi izvozno povpraevanje. Gospodarstvo je ob pomoi podpornih ukrepov ekonomskih politik ohranilo proizvodni potencial, hkrati pa so se izboljali obeti za prihodnjo rast. Tveganja pa ostajajo prisotna, saj je Slovenija jeseni vstopila v nov val pandemije. Ta je tudi zaradi primerjalno nije precepljenosti kot v veini drugih lanicah evrskega obmoja bolj intenziven. Vendar pa je zdaj na voljo cepivo, s imer se dele cepljenih, sicer poasi, a vendarle poveuje. Trenutno tudi ni indicev, da bi se zdravstvene razmere tako zaostrile, da bi bilo treba ponovno posegati po strogih omejevalnih ukrepih, ki bi prizadeli doloene dele gospodarstva, predvsem storitveni sektor. Hkrati so tevilne gospodarske panoge svoje poslovanje lahko prilagodile in jih tudi eventualni omejevalni ukrepi ne bi prizadeli tako kot v prejnjih epideminih valovih. Ti dejavniki izboljujejo obete za to in naslednje leto. Naa zadnja ocena, ki smo jo za evrsko obmoje naredili v okviru ECB, kae, da bo gospodarska rast dosegla 5 % in bi tudi v zaostrenem scenariju presegla 4 %. Ob splonem okrevanju svetovnega gospodarstva, predvsem naih trgovinskih partneric, zmanjanju negotovosti in pospeku zasebne potronje ob sprostitvi omejitvenih ukrepov pa so za Slovenijo obeti e bolji, saj je e naa junijska napoved kazala, da bo letonja gospodarska rast presegla 5 %. Zadnji ugodni podatki in tudi nekatere noveje napovedi pa nakazujejo, da bi lahko bila rast v letonjem letu tudi vija. Na srednji rok lahko gospodarsko rast sicer upoasnijo e omenjene motnje v dobavnih verigah. Uspeen dosedanji odziv politik na krizo Ukrepi, ki smo jih nosilci ekonomskih politik sprejemali v zadnjih osemnajstih mesecih, so se izkazali kot uspeni. Denarna politika je e dlje asa in bo e nekaj asa ostala spodbujevalno naravnana, s imer zagotavljamo obilno likvidnost in ugodne pogoje nanciranja tako bannemu in nebannemu sektorju kot tudi dravam Evrosistema. Hkrati pa se ob spodbudnih rezultatih postopoma umikajo nekateri drugi ukrepi, zlasti ukrepi skalne narave oziroma ukrepi, ki smo jih v asu zaostrenih razmer zaradi pandemije sprejemali za podporo gospodarstvu in za zagotavljanje nanne stabilnosti. Tako smo e v prvi polovici letonjega leta ocenili, da sistemski ukrep ugodneje regulatorne obravnave odlogov kreditnih obveznosti ni ve potreben. Prav tako pa smo se na podlagi poglobljenih analiz in skladno z odloitvami, ki smo jih sprejeli tudi na evropski ravni, konec avgusta odloili, da ne podaljujemo makrobonitetnega ukrepa, s katerim smo bankam in hranilnicam v zaostrenih gospodarskih razmerah do konca septembra omejili, lizing drubam pa priporoili, zmernost razdelitev dobikov, s imer se je okrepila odpornost nannega sistema na realizacijo tveganj, zlasti kreditnega. Poudarjena druga tveganja kot v blinji preteklosti V lui aktualnih razmer v irem makroekonomskem okolju ter stanja in trendov v nannem sistemu smo opravili redno presojo tveganj v nannem sistemu. Za celotno evropsko okolje, pa tudi specino za slovenski nanni sistem, ocenjujemo, da se sploen nivo tveganj nekoliko zmanjuje glede na nae ocene v preteklih nekaj kvartalih, hkrati pa ugotavljamo, da moramo nao pozornost usmeriti v druga tveganja kot v blinji preteklosti. Z izboljanjem makroekonomskih razmer in ponovnim oivljanjem gospodarstva se v evropskem okolju zmanjujeta makroekonomsko in kreditno tveganje, medtem ko so se v zadnjih mesecih poveala tveganja, ki izhajajo iz gibanj na nannih trgih in na nepremininskem trgu. Poveana so tveganja, ki izhajajo iz nepremininskega trga Slednje posebej velja tudi za Slovenijo, kjer zlasti prebivalstvo z izjemo nakupa nepreminin vidi le malo resnih alternativ hrambi privarevanih sredstev v obliki depozitov pri bankah. Medletna rast cen stanovanjskih nepreminin je v prvem etrtletju tega leta tako za skoraj dve odstotni toki presegla evropsko povpreje, pri emer je le osem drav Evropske unije imelo vije stopnje rasti. Rast cen stanovanjskih nepreminin pa se je v drugem etrtletju e pospeila in dosegla skoraj 10 %. Za Slovenijo sicer e vedno velja, da je rast cen na nepremininskem trgu ob sicer poveanem povpraevanju, ki ga nakazujejo tudi ugodni kazalniki zaupanja in spodbujajo nizke obrestne mere, uvajanje learin pri bankah ter ekspanzivna skalna politika, pomembno determinirana zlasti z omejeno ponudbo. Slovenija po tevilu stanovanj na tiso prebivalcev ostaja blizu dna drav Evropske unije, med najnijimi pa je tudi dele novogradenj v skupnem fondu nepreminin (za nami v obeh primerih zaostajajo le tiri drave, pri emer so vse, ki izstopajo po prvem kazalniku, pred Slovenijo po drugem, kar pomeni, da situacijo izboljujejo hitreje kot Slovenija). Investicije v stanovanjske nepreminine kot odstotek bruto domaega proizvoda so bile v letu 2020 kar tri odstotne toke pod povprejem Evropske unije, zaostanek pa je prisoten skozi dalje razdobje. Medtem ko je bila medletna rast proizvodnje v gradbenitvu v dravah Evropske unije v prvem etrtletju pozitivna (po zadnjih podatkih okvirno 2 %), je bila v Sloveniji negativna (skoraj -5 %), pri emer je samo sedem drav Evropske unije imelo ta parameter slabi od Slovenije. Srednjerono utegnejo ponudbo nekoliko okrepiti novogradnje, saj je bilo v prvi polovici leta 2021 izdano razmeroma visoko tevilo gradbenih dovoljenj za stanovanjske stavbe, med katerimi je tudi viji dele vestanovanjskih stavb kot v preteklih obdobjih. Glede na izjemno visok dele praznih nepreminin, najviji med lanicami Evropske unije (del teh nepreminin se sicer najbr oddaja), za katere so na voljo podatki, bi bile zelo koristne spodbude, ki bi te nepreminine pripeljale bodisi na (legalni) najemni bodisi na prodajni trg. Dohodkovno tveganje ostaja poviano Ne glede na upad splone ravni tveganj v nannem sistemu in manjemu premiku v hierarhiji oziroma pomembnosti posameznih tveganj v Sloveniji ostajajo prisotni doloeni izzivi iz preteklosti. Posledino so tudi nekatera tveganja naega bannega sistema nespremenjena oziroma imajo celo tendenco poveanja v blinji prihodnosti. V tem kontekstu je najbolj izrazito dohodkovno tveganje oziroma izziv zadostnega ustvarjanja dohodka bank, ki se nanaa na posamezne elemente ustvarjanja dohodka in obvladovanja strokov. Ta se povezuje tudi z odpornostjo bannega sistema, nenazadnje pa tudi s kreditnim tveganjem. V iskanju vijih donosnosti lahko namre banke zanejo prevzemati (pre)visoka tveganja. Za banni sistem je sicer kljuna zmonost ustvarjanja ustreznega dobika, ki ohranja kapitalsko kapaciteto bank tako ob normalnih gospodarskih razmerah in zmerni kreditni rasti kot tudi v stresnih razmerah. Neto obrestna mara slovenskih bank je bila v letu 2020 sicer na nivoju srednje vrednosti drav Evropske unije, vendar pa se je v zadnjih 15 letih zniala za skoraj eno odstotno toko z 2,44 % na 1,45 %. Poveevanje obsega kreditiranja v letih pred izbruhom epidemije ni bistveno okrepilo obrestnih prihodkov, neobrestni prihodki pa niso mogli nadomestiti izpada obrestnega dela, kar se odraa tudi v dobikonosnosti bannega sistema. Ta je pri nas na prvi pogled za evropske razmere odlina, saj so nae banke lani s preko desetodstotno povpreno donosnostjo dosegle prvo mesto v Evropski uniji. Vendar pa podroben vpogled v dejavnike te dobikonosnosti pokae precej slabo sliko: precejen del ustvarjenega dobika namre odpade na enkratne dejavnike. Lani je ve kot 40 % dobika izhajalo iz raunovodskega uinka zdruitve dveh bank, letos pa k ustvarjenemu dobiku prispeva razgradnja v preteklosti oblikovanih oslabitev in rezervacij. V letonjih estih mesecih so nae banke ustvarile ve kot 250 milijonov evrov dobika, vendar kar polovica poveanja dobika v primerjavi z lanskim letom, ko je ta znaal nekaj ve 130 milijonov evrov, izhaja iz razgradnje oslabitev in rezervacij. Povedano drugae: v letonjem letu bi donosnost na kapital slovenskih bank upadla na zgolj tretjino doseene, e e bi bile oslabitve in rezervacije na nivoju dolgoronega povpreja, brez izjemnih let njihovega oblikovanja ali razgradnje. Politika sproanja oslabitev je bila v prvem, manj optimistinem etrtletju tega leta med evropskimi bankami redka. Poleg slovenskega bannega sistema, ki je tudi lani oblikoval relativno malo oslabitev, so te v Evropski uniji sproali le e trije. Kreditno tveganje se je zmanjalo, vendar ni zanemarljivo Sproanje oslabitev in rezervacij sicer kae na zmanjano percepcijo kreditnega tveganja pri bankah. Tudi v Banki Slovenije kreditno tveganje ocenjujemo kot nekoliko zniano glede na pretekla obdobja, vendar e vedno poveano, saj je pri kazalnikih, ki jih spremljamo, prisotnih ve nasprotujoih si tendenc. Nedonosne izpostavljenosti bank se ob e tako nizkih nivojih e dodatno zniujejo, poleg tega banke prerazvrajo izpostavljenosti v skupine z manjim kreditnim tveganjem. Po drugi strani pa doloeni kazalniki kaejo na e vedno prisotno poveano kreditno tveganje. Delei nedonosnih posojil so bistveno veji pri posojilih z nezapadlimi odlogi kot v preostalem portfelju. Nadalje delei nedosnosnih posojil in posojil v skupini s poveanim kreditnim tveganjem naraajo v posameznih dejavnostih nenannih drub in pri nekaterih tipih komitentov oziroma posojil. Izstopajo dejavnosti, ki so jih ukrepi za omejitev epidemije bolj prizadeli, zlasti gostinstvo ter rekreacija, kultura in razvedrilne dejavnosti. Podobno velja za samostojne poklice (obrtnike) in potronika posojila. Dolgoroni izzivi, povezani s poslovnimi modeli bank Kratkorono lahko dobikonosnost bank kljub izboljanju razmer kroji tudi kreditno tveganje, medtem ko pa je za dolgorono uspeno poslovanje bank kljuno stabilno ustvarjanje neto dohodka. S tem pridemo do dileme, s katero se sooa celotno evropsko banno okolje: ali je banni posel e zanimiv za investitorje, ki zagotavljajo bannemu sistemu pomembno komponento  kapital? Ali bodo konkurenni pritiski, prilagoditve poslovanja bank in strategije lastnikov vodile v strukturne spremembe, ki bodo na dolgi rok zagotavljale stabilnost posameznih bank in celotnega nannega sistema? V Sloveniji imamo vsled relativno majhnega lokalnega trga bolj ali manj univerzalni poslovni model bannitva, pa vendarle se lahko tudi znotraj tega modela oblikujejo razlike, ki dobro sluijo vsem delenikom, predvsem uporabnikom bannih storitev in lastnikom. K znianju strokov poslovanja bank bo nedvomno prispevala konsolidacija naega bannega sistema, ki se dogaja e nekaj let, a lahko ob dodatnih zdruitvah e privede do optimuma oziroma meje, ko nadaljnja koncentracija ne bo ve prinaala prednosti za nanno stabilnost, uinkovitost in uporabnike bannih storitev. Prilonosti v digitalnem poslovanju in zeleni agendi Pandemija je pokazala, kje imajo banke e prilonosti, predvsem v smislu digitalnega poslovanja in druganih prodajnih kanalov. Podobno kot drugi gospodarski subjekti so se bile banke primorane v veji meri digitalizirati, e vedno pa v primerjavi z letom 2019, kot izhaja iz anketnih odgovorov bank samih, niso izkazale bistvenega napredka pri rabi sodobnih tehnologij. Sodelovanje s ntech podjetji lahko v primerjavi s konkuriranjem verjetno prinese ve prednosti, banke pa morajo ob tem izkoristiti svojo kljuno prednost pred subjekti, ki poslujejo predvsem ali izkljuno digitalno  osebno poznavanje svojih dolgoletnih strank, ki prinaa mehke informacije, ki jih na daljavo poslujoi subjekti ne premorejo. In nenazadnje je tu zelena agenda, ki je po umiritvi razmer zaradi pandemije ponovno v ospredju: evropske, tudi nae banke, lahko v specini strukturi nannega sistema, kjer prevladuje njihovo nanno posrednitvo, naredijo pomemben korak v smislu nae zelene preobrazbe. Banke so od stratekega razmisleka e naredile prve korake k razvoju zelenih produktov, vendar pa bodo morale v naslednjih letih e bolj podrobno razmisliti, katere projekte bodo nancirale, da bodo ohranjale zaupanje in ugled svojih lastnikov in strank pa tudi regulatorja. Nadzorniki in nosilci regulative oziroma pravil poslovanja bank se aktualnim trendom seveda prilagajamo oziroma v naem delovanju skuamo predvideti prihodnje izzive. Temu ustrezno se prilagaja naa pozornost v mikrobonitetnem nadzoru in bonitetnih pravilih, ki jih doloamo za poslovanje bank. Prilagaja pa se tudi naa makrobonitetna politika. Tako se je z oktobrom nabor makrobonitetnih ukrepov Banke Slovenije skril na tiri aktivne instrumente, katerih presojo potrebnosti in uinkovitosti e vedno redno opravljamo. Skrben razmislek o naboru ukrepov in fokusu naega delovanja vedno temelji na mandatu, ki nam je bil zaupan. Title: Speech at Slovenian Bankers Day
Subtitle: Governor Botjan Vasle was speaking to attendees of Slovenian Bankers Day, held on 24 November 2021 and organised by the Bank Association of Slovenia.
text: Governors speech at Slovenian Bankers Day 11/24/2021 / Public apperances Ladies and Gentlemen, My greetings to you all! I am delighted to be able to speak to you again at your annual gathering, although I would much rather be able to do this in real life. Alas, the worsening health situation makes this impossible. The great uncertainty surrounding the future evolution of the health situation is not affecting just our gatherings, but also the entire economic picture in Slovenia, in Europe and across the globe, and thus economic policy decisions too, including monetary policy, about which I will say more later. The Slovenian and euro area economies have recovered well in recent quarters: Slovenia has already surpassed its pre-pandemic GDP, while the euro area overall is very close to reaching it. The unemployment rate has fallen, and firms are again facing labour shortages. A key contribution to this positive picture has been made by economic policy: fiscal support to alleviate the impact of the pandemic amounted to more than 5% of GDP in Slovenia last year, and will be slightly lower this year at around 4% of GDP. Similar large-scale packages have been seen throughout the euro area. In the area of monetary policy too we have put in place the largest measures to date. There are two key measures: (i) the pandemic emergency purchase programme, in the amount of EUR 1,850 billion, and (ii) extremely low-cost long-term loans to banks in the amount of EUR 2,200 billion. The two measures together amounted to an incredible 36% of euro area GDP. But uncertainty remains high, with regard to the health picture and the economic picture alike. Despite the availability of vaccines, the health situation is worsening again, and the pandemic is once again curtailing economic activity. Further uncertainty relates to the normalisation of our policies, which we will have to embark on in the months ahead. Meanwhile other effects of the pandemic and the measures are becoming evident: after several years of low inflation, the rate passed 4% in the euro area and 3.5% in Slovenia in October. It will rise slightly further before the end of the year. For the moment the rise is largely being ascribed to temporary factors related to developments and measures during the early part of the crisis. For example, one significant factor is the tax changes in Germany: they had a significant impact on euro area inflation of around 0.6 percentage points, but the effect will drop out of the calculation in the early part of next year. In all likelihood it will be a similar case with oil prices: after sharp rises over the last year, in recent weeks they have shown signs of easing. Other factors, most notably the logjams in logistics and global supply chains are currently thought to be mostly temporary in nature, although they will continue to drive inflation for at least several more quarters. They might also have a longerterm impact on inflation, particularly if they lead to the shortening of production chains or the migration of production to closer locations that are less favourable in price terms. The rise in inflation is therefore not unexpected, but it has been more pronounced and more sustained than was anticipated at the beginning of the reversal. The key to future developments is what happens in two areas: the first is the expectations of firms and financial markets. The second, a related area, is the labour market, and the passthrough of higher prices into wage demands. These two factors could lead to inflation remaining above 2%, its core target level, for a sustained period. My message is the following: if the developments and projections indicate that higher inflation could become more persistent, we have sufficient instruments at our disposal to adequately address the inflationary pressures. The first monetary policy decisions will be taken soon, in mid-December, when we decide whether to end the pandemic emergency purchase programme, and whether to potentially make changes to the APP, i.e. our ordinary asset purchases, and also decide on the fate of the targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III). Here it is vital that the measures are designed to grant sufficient flexibility if the situation does not unfold in line with the core scenario. We must therefore ensure sufficient manoeuvring room in the event of a further deterioration in the pandemic, and thus in the economic situation, and also in the event of inflationary pressures lasting longer than anticipated and inflation being more sustained than expected. To close, allow me to touch on the banking system. The Slovenian banking system as a whole and the individual banks have survived the crisis to date without major upheaval. The key performance indicators have remained stable, and the changes in your activities have not differed significantly from those in other euro area countries. The anticipated normalisation of economic policy will also entail a change in your business environment, both in terms of financing and in terms of the take-up of risks, which during the crisis were to a great extent mitigated by economic policy measures. A major segment of your business activities will come to the fore again, namely lending to firms for their current operations and investment cycles, particularly in light of the broader commitments made by our country: (i) the transition to increased sustainability, and (ii) improvements in the area of digitalisation. And it is in this area that I see considerable opportunities for the Slovenian banking system, as bank lending to firms remains significantly below the euro area average, which is one of the key reasons why the banking system remains among the smallest in the euro area in terms of total size. This is in turn one of the factors in the modest operating profits recorded by the banks. At the ECB we have found banks to be profitable this year. The financial stability review released last week highlights that banks in the euro area differ greatly in their sources of profit. The first group, with relatively high profitability in the first half of this year, consists of banks whose increase in profits comes mainly from their primary business. The second group consists of banks with below-average profitability in the first half of the year: these banks recorded worse operating profits than last year, which they compensated for by releasing impairments and provisions and through other items. I should end by saying that these are the key challenges facing the Slovenian banking system. After the pandemic eases, the risks to economic growth abate and economic policy normalises, you will once again need to give them greater attention, and be ready for the various scenarios that lie ahead of us. Thank you for your time.

Title: Editorial to the special issue of Banni vestnik
Subtitle: The role, opportunities and challenges of the banking sector after the pandemic crisis.
text: Governors editorial to the special issue of Banni vestnik 11/25/2021 / Public apperances Published: Banni vestnik, November 2021 The recovery of our economies after a slowdown during the second and third waves of the COVID-19 pandemic has been faster than expected. More than two thirds of EU countries, including Slovenia, have already reached the pre-pandemic levels of GDP or will reach them later this year. However, uncertainty is still high and a surge in COVID-19 infections with increasing pressure on hospitals, further disruptions in global supply chains and aggravated labour shortages in some sectors have begun to stifle growth momentum and exert upward pressure on prices. Nevertheless, a significant part of the population has been vaccinated, so measures to contain the spread of COVID-19 infections can this time around be less restrictive, and businesses and consumers have adapted well to the new circumstances. Moreover, policymakers across several fields seem to agree in general that the unwinding of still abundant economic policy support should be gradual and well thought through, following the improvements in both health and economic situations. With strong and coherent support from monetary, prudential, fiscal and other policies and a significantly better starting position than before the previous financial crisis, the banking system in Slovenia and the EU in general has remained resilient. In addition to bank recapitalisations and the resolution of non-performing loans (NPLs) after the previous crisis, the strengthening of banking regulation and supervision, which are now much more uniform across Europe, played a particularly important role. All of this has enabled banks to continue lending to the real economy and avoid the credit crunch we have witnessed in the previous financial crisis. While banks have increased the share of forborne loans in this crisis, the NPL ratio has surprisingly fallen further at the level of the system. In addition, this year most Slovenian and to a lesser extent some other European banks have begun to make impairment releases, which provided a short-term boost to their profitability. Nevertheless, we call on banks to be vigilant and prudent, as all the consequences of the crisis are not yet visible and the increased credit and some other risks might be realised with a lag, which will probably be longer than usual given the unprecedented policy support. Although the pandemic crisis is still at the forefront of our deliberations and policy actions, we are already focusing our attention on structural challenges that will become more apparent again when the crisis is over. Like many European banks, their Slovenian counterparts are about to confront subdued profitability, which in the years before the crisis and this year was masked by one-off revenues and the release of impairments and provisions. The prolonged period of low interest rates and the rise of non-bank financial intermediation are particularly challenging for banks that are more reliant on traditional banking activities, including Slovenian banks and many others in the CEE region. As a source of strengthening and attracting capital, bank profitability will be playing important role in light of the expected implementation of the renewed Basel III standards, more systematic consideration of climate risks and increased needs for modernisation of technology amidst growing competition from fintech and other nonbanks. Bettercapitalised banks generally lend more, as confirmed in the current crisis for the euro banks. Quite the opposite holds true for corporate lending by Slovenian banks, whose capital position is otherwise solid. With the relatively weak corporate demand for loans, more than a decade-long trend of lower corporate lending (relative to GDP) than in the euro area thus continues. In the need for a strong and resilient European banking system, which will be able to contribute to financing the recovery, accelerated digitisation and greening of our economies, it is important that at the EU level we continue with banking reforms initiated after the previous financial crisis, which have shown good results during this crisis. Pan-European efforts to improve the efficiency of capital allocation, to unify the European financial services market and create a capital market union are likely to gradually diversify the economy's funding instruments and sources. This brings new opportunities and challenges for banks, which will be easier to seize and manage as the banking sector continues to consolidate. In addition, activities to maintain the economic role and stability of Slovenian banks which have undergone significant structural changes in the last 15 years -should include work on sustainability of business models, along with reducing income risk and developing banking products, further digitisation and efficiency gains, and addressing the large maturity gap between bank assets and liabilities.

Title: Article by Deputy Governor Primo Dolenc in Manager magazine
Subtitle: Content  in Slovene only.
text: Article by Deputy Governor Primoz Dolenc in Manager magazine 12/24/2021 / Public apperances Objavljeno: Manager, 24. december 2021 On the threshold of "new normality"? When I got a friendly invitation from Financ to contribute to this year's Christmas edition of the publication, I first thought that again everything would revolve around a word that has been following us for almost a full second year: coronavirus and its associated consequences. When I finished preparing the paper, it turned out to be true, but unlike in the past year, this word is accompanied by much more optimism. And it is precisely optimism that is the right mood that is supposed to mark the end of the year and accompany us to new challenges in the coming year. A year is therefore coming to an end, which, much to the extent that was marked by current epidemiological conditions, is largely marked as last year. However, if we look to the future at the end of this year, we can conclude that this time we are accompanied by much less uncertainty than at this time last year. Notwithstanding the emergence of ever-new strains of the virus, which, while maintaining a certain amount of uncertainty, is the fact that health care in this area has taken a huge step forward, both in the form of vaccines and the latest medicines. This is a key factor in the current situation, the less likely likelihood of the need to re-restrict public life and, he does, the economic recovery. Thus, today we can have a greater degree of confidence in the future period, at least in economic terms, less marked by difficult health conditions, so we can once again focus on the challenges, dilemmas and, above all, the opportunities that the future brings. If we look at the expiry year or two, we can conclude that the first pandemic shock as an economy has gone quite well. Last year was a period when virtually all of us were looking for solutions and adjustments to the situation, and economic policymakers faced a challenge that was foreign to us: how do we respond to the tightened economic situation, not to say a serious crisis that does not arise from the real economy, where the cause is not a disparity in financial markets or what is not caused by economic operators with irresponsible behaviour, exogenously induced health crisis with wider consequences. In short, it was a rather unknown area where we could not lean on serious past practices or experiences. However, a general consensus was quickly formed that the actions of economic policy makers must be clear, swift, determined and, above all, coordinated, while it is difficult to hope for their effectiveness. And these measures must be broad-based and coordinated, not only nationally, but transnationally, and we may need to go beyond certain dogmas of the past that would limit more decisive action. I mean, i mean that fiscal measures were not limited by the relatively rigid constraints that apply to fiscal policy for the euro area Member States, monetary policy was not limited by standard measures and instruments and the like. Although economists like to intervene in our estimates for as long as possible data series, we can still estimate, based on current facts, that, according to the first forecasts, the consequences of the crisis will not be as drastic as the recovery, and the duration of the recovery was significantly shorter than initially suggested. Of course, our first impact and duration assessments were based on assumptions about the absence of economic policy stimulus measures and the slow adjustment of economic operators to the new situation. In fact, during this period, there was a positive effect of both: as mentioned above, all economic policies have responded decisively, quickly and harmonisedly, and it has once again shown that humans are adaptive beings: both the population and the economy have adapted quite well to the new situation during the duration of the pandemic. Solutions came to the fore that we didn't even think about a few years ago. Slovenia is no exception here. If we look at the specific data, we can see that good trends continue in our country. Thus, data on the trend of gross domestic product in Slovenia, on labour market conditions, etc. show. To set out only two encouraging facts: (i) in the third quarter of this year gross domestic product growth was high, as much as 5%, and (ii) economic activity has already exceeded pre-crisis levels. Before the summer, we had forecast economic growth of 5.2 per cent this year in our macroeconomic projections. However, developments since then indicate that this will be even higher this year, almost 7%, and favourable forecasts for the coming years are also favourable. Thus, it can be concluded that, despite the extraordinary deviation from the ferry line of the movement of gross domestic product, there is a strong likelihood that we will return to the 2019 route in a relatively short period. Figure 1: Real GDP level in the forecast period Source: SORS, calculations of Banka Slovenije. In addition to coronavirus, inflation has been at the forefront of our attention in recent times. The latest data show that inflation in Slovenia has approached 5%; a closer look at its structure shows that energy prices contributed more than half of the impact to inflation. Energy prices fell dramatically in the early months of the pandemic: the price of Brent oil fell more than 50% below the 40 EUD per barrel in a good year. This led to deflation over the course of most of last year, and this year average prices returned to the average level of 2019, and in the latter part of this year they were even significantly above that level. Therefore, the "statistical/technical" effect on elevated inflation is understandable. In this context, the current rise in inflation is of a short-term nature and, while stabilizing the energy market situation, we can expect inflation to persist at higher levels for the next few months, but should return to significantly lower levels over the course of next year. Of course, there are certain risks of a longer-term nature, such as the continuation of tightened conditions in global supply chains, the potential transfer of currently elevated price levels to longer-term inflation expectations of households, businesses and financial markets, and labour market conditions, and the impact on domestic price factors will also have a fiscal policy stance. Central banks are therefore particularly closely monitoring all these risks and  if they are put into effect  we will use all the instruments at our disposal to prevent longer-term deviations in inflation or to maintain price stability. At the same time, as in health care, where economists point out that the current epidemic is taking a look at other current health challenges, we are pushing the structural challenges of the economy, which remain unresolved or deepening. There is undoubtedly a labour market among them. Slovenia entered the latest crisis with a relatively favourable labour market situation in terms of the number of unemployed and persons in employment. More than that: by the end of 2019 Slovenia was characterised by a marked labour shortage, which our companies had to deal with by employing foreigners (at that time, about seven were new employees). While the number of unemployed people increased slightly during the first and second wave of the pandemic, this year we are monitoring a marked decline in the current 65,000 from a peak of 90,000. What will happen in the period ahead? According to the data, almost half of companies in the construction sector, one third of manufacturing enterprises and one fifth of enterprises in services (excluding trade) are already at risk of shortages. Thus, labour will continue to be a limiting factor in the near future, which could result in additional wage pressures. We cannot even pass the fact that the current number of employees in Slovenia is historically high. Figure 2: Employment and survey unemployment Source: SORS, calculations of Banka Slovenije. The second trend we have been following in recent months is the pronounced pressures on the real estate market, especially the residential property market. In Slovenia, property prices have been on the rise for several years (the market bottomed out in 2014 and 2015, after the peak of the economic and financial crisis). In Banka Slovenije we monitor this situation through various indicators and the latest data show that in most of these we are already approaching if we have not even exceeded the limit of relative overvaluation. The figure shown applies to Slovenia as a whole, and it is clear that the pressures are strongest in major cities and on the coast. In the 1960s, the united States and the United States were the first countries to have a similar situation. Traditionally in Slovenia, prices on the property market are driven by limiting factors on the supply side, as the supply of suitable building areas and dwellings in the desired locations is quite limited for various reasons. This may soften construction slightly, following the increased number of building permits issued in recent months, but there will be a back-up effect. But there are also factors on the demand side. In recent years, and in recent months, when, despite the pandemic, labour market conditions have remained relatively favourable with all economic policy measures, while at the same time there has been limited spending due to restrictive measures, the volume of household deposits has increased significantly. With low deposit rates and a lack of most "acceptable" investment opportunities, many people reach for a familiar alternative: buying a flat as an investment. Although non-traditional, however  some companies are thinking similarly recently. Adding to this the accelerated marketing of residential loans by the banking sector, where lending has also accelerated in recent months, the result is expected. 2022 will therefore be groundbreaking in a certain sense: a "new normality" is being formed slowly but surely between us. The realisation that the world will no longer be the same as it was before the epidemic is becoming more common. At least in view of the macroeconomic situation and forecasts, it can be said that, in many respects, we are returning to established rails, but on the other hand, the fact is that certain habits and established business practices will be different in the future. And it is in them that we can find new ideas and possibilities of development, both in private and business life.
text_original: Article by Deputy Governor Primo Dolenc in Manager magazine 12/24/2021 / Public apperances Objavljeno: Manager, 24. december 2021 Na pragu "nove normalnosti"? Ko sem dobil prijazno povabilo Financ, da prispevam k letonji boini izdaji publikacije, sem najprej pomislil, da se bo ponovno vse vrtelo okoli besede, ki nas spremlja e skoraj polno drugo leto: koronavirusa in z njim povezanih posledic. Ko sem pripravo prispevka dokonal, se je izkazalo, da to sicer dri, vendar za razliko od preteklega leta to besedo spremlja tudi precej ve optimizma. In ravno optimizem je tisto pravo razpoloenje, ki naj bi zaznamovalo zakljuujoe se leto in nas v prihajajoem letu pospremilo novim izzivom nasproti. Zakljuuje se torej leto, ki je bilo podobno kot lansko leto v preteni meri zaznamovano z aktualnimi epidemiolokimi razmerami. Vendar, e se ob zakljuku letonjega leta uzremo v prihodnost, lahko sklenemo, da nas tokrat spremlja precej manja negotovost kot lansko leto ob tem asu. Ne glede na pojave vedno novih sevov virusa, ki sicer ohranjajo doloeno mero negotovosti, je dejstvo, da je zdravstvo na tem podroju naredilo ogromen korak naprej, in sicer tako v obliki cepiv, kakor tudi najnovejih zdravil. To je v zdajnjih razmerah kljuni dejavnik manje verjetnosti potrebe po ponovnem obsenejem omejevanju javnega ivljenja, s tem pa tudi gospodarskega okrevanja. Tako imamo lahko danes vejo mero zaupanja v to, da bodo prihodnje obdobje vsaj v gospodarskem smislu manj zaznamovale oteene zdravstvene razmere, zato se lahko ponovno posveamo izzivom, dilemam, predvsem pa prilonostim, ki jih prinaa prihodnost. e se vendarle ozremo na iztekajoe se leto ali dve, lahko sklenemo, da smo prvi ok zaradi pandemije kot ekonomija precej dobro preli. Lansko leto je bilo obdobje, ko smo praktino vsi iskali reitve in prilagoditve za nastalo situacijo, nosilci ekonomskih politik pa smo se spopadali z izzivom, ki nam je bil tuj: kako naj se odzovemo na zaostrene gospodarske razmere, da ne reem resno krizo, ki ne izhaja iz realnega gospodarstva, kjer vzrok niso neskladja na nannih trgih ali kar niso povzroili ekonomski subjekti z neodgovornim ravnanjem, ampak iz eksogeno povzroene zdravstvene krize s irimi posledicami. lo je skratka za precej nepoznano podroje, kjer se nismo mogli nasloniti na resne pretekle prakse ali izkunje. Vendar se je hitro oblikovalo splono soglasje, da morajo biti ukrepi nosilcev ekonomskih politik jasni, hitri, odloni in predvsem usklajeni, sicer teko upamo na njihovo uinkovitost. In ti ukrepi morajo biti iroko zasnovani in koordinirani, ne zgolj nacionalno, ampak nadnacionalno, hkrati pa moramo morda presei doloene dogme iz preteklosti, ki bi omejevale odloneje ukrepanje. S tem mislim na to, da se skalni ukrepi niso omejevali z relativno rigidnimi omejitvami, ki za skalno politiko veljajo za drave lanice evro obmoja, denarna politika se ni omejevala s standardnimi ukrepi in instrumenti in podobno. eprav ekonomisti za bolj trdno oporo pri svojih ocenah radi posegamo po im daljih asovnih serijah podatkov, pa vseeno lahko na podlagi trenutnih dejstev ocenimo, da glede na prve napovedi posledice krize ne bodo tako drastine, pa tudi trajanje okrevanja je bilo oz. bo bistveno kraje, kot je sprva kazalo. Seveda so nae prve ocene uinkov in trajanja temeljile na predpostavkah odsotnosti spodbujevalnih ukrepov ekonomskih politik in poasnemu prilagajanju ekonomskim subjektom novim razmeram. Dejansko pa je v tem obdobju prilo do pozitivnega uinka obojega: kot e omenjeno, so se vse ekonomske politike odzvale odlono, hitro in usklajeno, pa se je ponovno pokazalo, da smo ljudje prilagodljiva bitja: tako prebivalstvo kot gospodarstvo so se na nove razmere v asu trajanja pandemije precej dobro prilagodili. Na dan so prile reitve, na katere pred nekaj leti nismo niti pomislili. Slovenija pri tem ni nobena izjema. e se ozremo na konkretne podatke, lahko ugotovimo, da se tudi pri nas ugodna gibanja nadaljujejo. Tako kaejo podatki o gibanju bruto domaega proizvoda v Sloveniji, o razmerah na trgu dela ipd. e nanizam samo dve spodbudni dejstvi: (i) v tretjem etrtletju letonjega leta je bila rast bruto domaega proizvoda visoka, kar petodstotna, in (ii) gospodarska aktivnost pa je e presegla predkrizno raven. Pred poletjem smo v naih makroekonomskih projekcijah napovedali, da bo gospodarska rast letos znaala 5,2 odstotka. Vendar razvoj dogodkov od tedaj dalje kae, da bo ta v letonjem letu e vija, skoraj 7-odstotna, ugodne pa so napovedi tudi za prihodnja leta. Tako lahko sklenemo, da kljub izrednemu odklonu od trajektorije gibanja bruto domaega proizvoda obstaja velika verjetnost, da se bomo na zartano pot iz leta 2019 vrnili v relativno kratkem obdobju. Slika 1: Raven realnega BDP v napovednem obdobju Vir: SURS, prerauni Banke Slovenije. Poleg koronavirusa se v ospredje nae pozornosti v zadnjem obdobju pojavlja inacija. Zadnji podatki namre kaejo, da se je inacija v Sloveniji pribliala petim odstotkom; podrobneji vpogled v njeno strukturo pokae, da so cene energentov k inaciji prispevale ve kot polovico uinka. Cene energentov so se namre v zaetnih mesecih pandemije izjemno zniale: cena nafte Brent je v dobrem letu upadla za ve kot 50 % pod 40 EUD za sodek. To je vodilo v deacijo tekom veine lanskega leta, letos pa so se povprene cene vrnile na povpreno raven iz leta 2019, v zadnjem delu letonjega leta pa so bile celo bistveno nad to ravnjo. Zato je statistini/tehnini uinek na poviano inacijo razumljiv. V tem smislu je trenutni porast inacije kratkorone narave in lahko ob stabilizaciji razmer na trgu energentov priakujemo, da bo inacija pri vijih ravneh sicer e vztrajala nekaj naslednjih mesecev, vendar bi se morala tekom naslednjega leta vrniti na obutno nije ravni. Seveda pa se pri tem pojavljajo doloena tveganja dolgoroneje narave, kot so nadaljevanje zaostrenih razmer v globalnih dobavnih verigah, potencialni prenos trenutno zvianih ravni cen v dolgoroneja inacijska priakovanja gospodinjstev, podjetij in nannih trgov ter razmere na trgu dela, vpliv na domae cenovne dejavnike bo imela tudi naravnanost skalne politike. Centralne banke zato e posebej pozorno spremljamo vsa ta tveganja in bomo  e se bodo zaela udejanjati  uporabili vse instrumente, ki jih imamo na voljo, da prepreimo dolgoroneje odklone v inaciji oz. ohranimo stabilnost na podroju cen. Ob tem pa tudi ekonomisti podobno kot v zdravstvu, kjer opozarjajo, da aktualna epidemija zastira pogled na druge aktualne izzive v zdravstvu, vse glasneje v ospredje ponovno potiskamo strukturne izzive gospodarstva, ki ostajajo nereeni oz. se e poglabljajo. Med njimi je nedvomno trg dela. V zadnjo krizo je Slovenija vstopila z relativno ugodnim stanjem na trgu dela, kar se tie tevila brezposelnih in delovno aktivnih. Celo ve: e do konca leta 2019 je bilo za Slovenijo znailno izrazito pomanjkanje delovne sile, kar so morala naa podjetja reevati z zaposlovanjem tujcev (takrat je bilo od desetih novo zaposlenih priblino sedem tujcev). V asu prvega in drugega vala pandemije je sicer tevilo brezposelnih nekoliko poraslo, ampak v letonjem letu iz vrha pri 90 tisoih spremljamo izrazit upad na trenutnih 65 tiso. Kako bo v prihodnjem obdobju? Kot kaejo podatki, pomanjkanje delavcev preti e skoraj polovici podjetij iz gradbenega sektorja, eni tretjini podjetij iz predelovalnih dejavnosti in eni petini podjetij iz storitvenih dejavnosti (brez trgovine). Tako bo delovna sila omejitveni dejavnik tudi v blinji prihodnosti, kar bi lahko imelo za posledico dodatne plane pritiske. Ne moremo namre niti mimo dejstva, da je trenutno tevilo zaposlenih v Sloveniji zgodovinsko visoko. Slika 2: Zaposlenost in anketna brezposelnost Vir: SURS, prerauni Banke Slovenije. Drugi trend, ki ga spremljamo v zadnjih mesecih, pa so izraziti pritiski na nepremininskem trgu, posebej trgu stanovanjskih nepreminin. V Sloveniji so cene nepreminin v porastu e nekaj let (trg je dno dosegel v letih 2014 in 2015, po vrhuncu ekonomsko-nanne krize). V Banki Slovenije te razmere spremljamo preko razlinih kazalnikov in zadnji podatki kaejo, da se po veini izmed teh e pribliujemo, e nismo celo presegli mejo relativne precenjenosti. Prikazana slika velja sicer za Slovenijo kot celoto, pri emer je jasno, da so pritiski najmoneji v vejih mestih in na obali. Taknim razmeram, ki v Sloveniji niso unikatne, saj lahko podobna gibanja opazujemo tudi v drugih dravah Evropske unije, botruje ve dejavnikov. Tradicionalno v Sloveniji cene na trgu nepreminin poganjajo omejitveni dejavniki na ponudbeni strani, saj je ponudba primernih zazidalnih povrin in stanovanj na elenih lokacijah iz razlinih razlogov precej omejena. To bodo morda nekoliko omilile gradnje, ki bodo sledile poveanemu tevilu izdanih gradbenih dovoljenj v zadnjih mesecih, vendar bo priel uinek z zamikom. So pa tudi dejavniki na strani povpraevanja. V zadnjih letih, posebej pa v zadnjih mesecih, ko so kljub pandemiji razmere na trgu dela ob vseh ukrepih ekonomskih politik ostale razmeroma ugodne, hkrati pa je bilo zaradi omejitvenih ukrepov troenje omejeno, se je obseg vlog gospodinjstev znatno poveal. Ob nizkih depozitnih obrestnih merah in pomanjkanju veini sprejemljivih investicijskih prilonosti, marsikdo posee po nam znani alternativi: nakupu stanovanja kot investiciji. eprav netradicionalno, pa vendarle  podobno zadnje ase razmiljajo tudi doloena podjetja. e temu dodamo e pospeeno trenje stanovanjskih posojil s strani bannega sektorja, kjer se je kreditiranje v zadnjih mesecih tudi pospeilo, je rezultat priakovan. Leto 2022 bo torej v doloenem smislu torej prelomno: poasi, vendar zanesljivo se med nami oblikuje nova normalnost. Vse pogosteje je namre spoznanje, da svet ne bo ve taken, kot je bil pred epidemijo. Vsaj glede na makroekonomsko stanje in napovedi lahko sicer reemo, da se z ve vidikov vraamo na ustaljene tirnice, po drugi strani pa je dejstvo, da bodo doloene navade in ustaljene poslovne prakse v bodoe drugane. In prav v njih lahko najdemo nove ideje in monosti razvoja, tako v zasebnem kot poslovnem ivljenju.

Title: The magazine was published at the Eurofi Financial Forum 2022, which takes place in Paris from 23 to 25 February 2022.
text: BANKA SLOVENIJE EVROSISTEM Article by Governor Bostjan Vasle in Eurofi magazine 02/23/2022 / Public apperances Published: Eurofi magazine, February 2022 Transition from crisis mode to a gradual normalisation of monetary policy by Bostjan Vasle, Governor of Banka Slovenije Key sentence: We need to start rebuilding the monetary policy space to be ready for the next business cycle. Less than two years into the pandemic, the euro area economy has returned to the pre-crisis level of activity, though the recovery has been incomplete in some sectors and countries. With a rapid and comprehensive response of monetary, fiscal and other policies to a once-in-a-lifetime shock, we prevented the free fall of the economy and helped to preserve financial stability and protect productive potential. As our interest rates were near the effective lower bound, the Eurosystem has resorted to unconventional monetary measures, launching tailor-made instruments to leave no one behind. With the roughly simultaneous reopening of economies and relatively robust household incomes, backed by fiscal and other measures, regional and global demand rebounded strongly. This led to supply-chain bottlenecks and shortages of different goods, ranging from energy and construction materials to computer chips, and brought about soaring prices. The pick-up of inflation in the euro area and elsewhere was not unexpected, considering the low reference base in 2020 and the impact of pandemic-driven one-offs and other presumably short-term factors. In an effort to secure the uncertain recovery, we last year had good reasons to tolerate supply-driven spike of inflation - after a decade of it falling short of the target set. However, Eurozone inflation prints kept surpassing our projections in recent months. Energy inflation and consequently headline inflation exceeded their highest levels since the introduction of the euro. Global supply chain disruptions have proven more sustained, while Europe also grapples with the energy supply crunch, aggravated by geopolitical developments and the EUs own climate-related policies. With the persistence of these factors, price growth has been gradually spilling over into a wider range of products, bringing core inflation rate on par with its previous 20-year peak. Elevated inflation is set to persist well into 2022, longer than previously expected. The development of the pandemic and thus the duration of disruptions in supply chains are still uncertain. At the same time, various structural policies and geopolitical disputes indicate no immediate relief in energy prices. Longer spell of higher inflation increases the danger of it becoming more entrenched and broad-based. Studies show that euro area economies tend to be at risk of price hikes leading to increased wage pressures. In addition, expectations of future inflation, an important determinant of inflation, are highly state dependent and tend to react strongly to current inflation. Higher inflation, even if caused by external factors, could therefore result in a feed-back loop through higher wages and increased inflation expectations. Our monetary policy focus should therefore be on identifying early signs of increased wage pressures or the de- anchoring of inflation expectations above our target. In addition to the surge in consumer prices, some of the unintended consequences of our policies are also weighing heavily on our decisions. In a low-yield environment investors are seeking yields in risker segments of the markets, or are pushing the prices of some investment possibilities, like housing, into levels where abrupt repricing could pose a threat to the macroeconomic environment. Furthermore, our maintaining of favourable financing conditions across all sectors and jurisdictions during the pandemic has contributed to increased debt levels in these sectors, hence inducing refinancing risk. Macroprudential policies with capital- and borrower-based tools are an important line of defence, but they focus primarily on the banking sector and are not all powerful. The longer the highly accommodative policy is maintained, the more pronounced these risks become, and the more painful the normalisation process may have to be. Given these considerations, the time seems right for our monetary policy to move out of crisis mode and start the process of gradual normalisation. With the return of economic activity to the pre-crisis level, looming labour shortages and in part structural pressures on energy prices, our monetary policy needs to start rebuilding its space to be ready to respond to the next business cycle. However, this has to be a gradual and predictable path, in order not to pull the rug from underneath a more complete recovery in the context of an enduring pandemic. The decisions at our previous monetary policy meetings have laid the necessary groundwork to implement such an approach. Magazine Eurofi magazine is available on thelink.

Title: Address by Tina umer, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Slovenia, at the Government Borrowers Forum 2022The event was organised by the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Slovenia. The text is only available in English.
text: BANKA SLOVENIJE EVROSISTEM Keynote speech by Tina Zumer, Deputy Governor of Banka Slovenije, at the Government Borrowers Forum 2022 06/01/2022 / Public apperances Time for interest rate normalisation Dear ladies and gentlemen, dear speakers and organisers of this event, dear guests, good morning. It is with great pleasure that I am addressing you today - especially as I can do it in person. Over the last two years, face-to-face interaction has gained my appreciation. With all the uncertainties surrounding the economy and high volatility in financial markets in recent months, the time is particularly appropriate for engaging with treasurers, investors, bankers and other financial experts. It will be interesting to hear your views on various challenging issues - such as the geopolitical and energy crises, climate change and global health risks - and your expectations regarding macroeconomic and financial developments. As we are continuing with the normalisation of our monetary policy and approaching the first rise in the ECB interest rates since 2011, I will devote an important part of my speech today to policy making, in particular to monetary policy decisions and monetary-fiscal interaction. As these depend on economic and financial developments and outlook, let me start by outlining the recent economic situation. After the greatest global health shock in our lives, triggering a sudden and deep recession, most euro area economies recovered faster than expected In the first quarter of this year, the output in the euro area exceeded the pre- pandemic level by 0.5%, while it was more than 7% higher in Slovenia. A rapid and comprehensive policy response - including monetary and fiscal policies - combined with the progress in vaccination, have been instrumental in the speedy recovery. Together we prevented the free fall of the economy and helped to preserve financial stability and protect productive potential. As our interest rates were near the effective lower bound, the Eurosystem resorted to unconventional monetary policy measures in response to the pandemic, launching tailor-made instruments to leave no country behind. For example, we launched a new asset purchase programme - the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP) - and a new series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III). Strong economic rebound after the reopening of the economies lead to global shortages of different goods and, in turn, the pick-up of inflation, as COVID-related supply disruptions continued. An increase in inflation was not unexpected, considering the low reference base in 2020, but turned out to be more significant, broader and more persistent. For Slovenia, the broadening of inflationary pressures is well illustrated by the fact that the share of items in the HICP basket with more than 5% price growth increased from around 20% in the autumn of last year to over 60% in April. However, even before the Russian invasion of Ukraine there were signs that it will take longer for inflation to moderate than projected last year. The war and anti-Russia sanctions on top of new waves of COVID infections exacerbated global supply constraints. This caused the euro area and global inflation to surge further, and accelerated the process of winding down of the historic monetary stimulus globally. In turn, the worry arose whether all these developments could tip our economies into a recession, as shown - for example - by the rising number of Google searches for the word recession. The topic was also high on the agenda at the recent gathering in Davos. Within the Eurosystem, we are in the process of preparing new macroeconomic projections, which we will publish next week.[1] As already revealed publicly, the recession is not part of the baseline scenario that is the most likely to materialise. While there are some clouds gathering over the economy, we do not currently see a storm. Despite the increased cost of living and the devastating war at the door of Europe, the economic activity in the euro area expanded further in the first quarter. The incoming high frequency and first hard data also bode quite well for the second quarter. In particular, the number of people employed in the euro area is at a record high, and the unemployment rate hit new low in May. The Eurozone Purchasing Manager Index (PMI) declined somewhat in May but still signals growth. Consumer confidence, which deteriorated sharply after the Russian invasion, broadly stabilised in May, while at the same time households have accumulated considerable savings during the pandemic. However, beyond the second quarter, the uncertainty is greater and there are considerable economic risks due to the war and geopolitical tensions. In sum, we are currently in an unusual and challenging situation. According to many economic indicators - such as employment, labour shortages, capacity utilisation in manufacturing, elevated inflation and over-valuation of housing markets - we are high in the business cycle At the same time, our monetary policy is still exceptionally accommodative after coping with the lengthy period of deflationary pressures and the pandemic shock. Let me now turn to inflation, the key variable of our monetary policy. A series of supply-side disruptions and a rapid recovery in global demand have pushed inflation significantly above our medium-term target of 2%, after almost a decade of too-low inflation.
